summaryEn: The company behind 85°C, the bakery-cafe chain that conquered Taiwan, expanded into China and America — and has just closed roughly 180 of its 440 Chinese stores after four consecutive years of losses there, while its US business grows at double digits.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; F&B-chain framing — the brand, US double-digit growth, fourth consecutive quarter of Taiwanese growth and the China restructuring credited as a decisive move, but the NT$1bn+ impairment, FY2025 loss, suspended dividend, four years of China losses and still-declining revenue stated plainly; P/E of 0.00 stripped as meaningless on a loss; founding/listing years left null as unverified; sector Tourism & Leisure → Restaurants & Bakery)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Gourmet Master (美食-KY, TWSE: 2723) is the company behind **85°C (85度C)** — the bakery-cafe chain whose combination of cheap sea-salt coffee and affordable cakes made it a fixture of Taiwanese daily life, and which then expanded into **mainland China and the United States**. It is a Cayman-registered ("KY") company listed in Taipei, and it adds a business type this collection lacked: a **restaurant and bakery chain with major overseas exposure** — a deliberate contrast to Wowprime, whose restaurants are domestically focused.

Its recent history is a case study in **retreating from a market that did not work**. In the third quarter of 2025 the company took a **loss of NT$1.09bn — a quarterly loss of NT$6.06 per share** — after deciding to close **roughly 180 of its approximately 440 stores in mainland China**, along with **two central kitchens** (in Beijing, Shandong, Chengdu and Chongqing) and to cut its physical distribution centres **from eight to three**, recognising **over NT$1bn of one-time impairment**. That charge turned the year negative: annual EPS went **NT$2.69 (FY2022) → 4.20 (FY2023) → 3.28 (FY2024) → −NT$2.47 (FY2025)**, and **the dividend was suspended** after NT$3.0 for 2024.

What makes the story more interesting than a simple failure is **how differently its three markets are performing**. Measured in local currency, the **United States grew at double digits**, **Taiwan recorded its fourth consecutive quarter of growth**, and **mainland China fell 20%** amid intense competition and weak consumer spending. China had been **loss-making for four consecutive years**; closing 40% of the store base is the company's attempt to end that.

The early evidence is tentatively encouraging: **2026Q1 returned to profit at NT$1.31 per share**, with operating margin recovering to **8.0%** and gross margin to **61.1%**, while the revenue decline narrowed from **−20.7% in March to −4.2% in June** — smaller, because there are fewer stores. The stock trades at **NT$61.90, essentially at book value (P/B 1.08×)**, with no dividend. The honest read: **a strong brand with a genuinely healthy US and Taiwanese business, finally amputating a Chinese operation that lost money for four years — early signs of repair, but the recovery is one quarter old and the shares pay nothing while it proves itself.**

85°C was built on a simple and very effective idea: sell **coffee at a price people would pay every day, and cakes good enough to justify the trip** — from bright, high-traffic stores open long hours. The name refers to the temperature at which coffee is said to taste best. In Taiwan the formula worked spectacularly: the chain became ubiquitous, its sea-salt coffee a national habit, and its bakery counters a default for birthday cakes and office snacks.

Success at home led to the ambition that defines the company's recent history: **expansion into mainland China**. The logic was irresistible on paper — the same product, a market fifty times larger, and a Taiwanese brand with genuine consumer appeal. The chain grew to around **440 stores in China**. It also expanded into the **United States**, serving both Asian-American communities and a broader market, where the bakery-cafe format had less direct competition.

China proved far harder than the arithmetic suggested. Domestic Chinese chains multiplied, coffee prices collapsed under aggressive local competition, consumer spending weakened, and the cost of operating a physical store network across widely separated regions — Beijing, Shandong, Chengdu, Chongqing — proved punishing. The business **lost money for four consecutive years**.

The decision announced in 2025 was, by the standards of corporate retreats, decisive: **close roughly 180 of the 440 Chinese stores and two central kitchens, and consolidate distribution centres from eight to three**, taking **over NT$1bn of impairment** in a single quarter. It produced the largest quarterly loss in the company's history — **NT$6.06 per share** — and the suspension of a dividend that had been paid for years. The bet is that a smaller Chinese business, concentrated where it works, can stop consuming the profits that Taiwan and the United States generate.

- **2000s** — 85°C establishes itself in Taiwan with an affordable coffee-and-bakery format; becomes a nationwide fixture. Lists in Taipei as a Cayman-registered ("KY") company.
- **2010s** — Expands aggressively into **mainland China** (reaching roughly 440 stores) and into the **United States**.
- **2021–2024** — The **China business loses money for four consecutive years** amid intense local competition and weakening consumer spending; group EPS nonetheless holds up on Taiwan and US strength: **NT$2.69 (FY2022) → 4.20 (FY2023) → 3.28 (FY2024)**.
- **2025Q3** — **The reckoning**: decision to close **~180 of ~440 China stores** and **2 central kitchens**, cutting distribution centres **from 8 to 3**; over **NT$1bn of one-time impairment**; quarterly loss **NT$1.09bn (EPS −6.06)**.
- **2025 (full year)** — **EPS −NT$2.47**; **dividend suspended** after NT$3.0 for 2024. Regional split: **US double-digit growth, Taiwan a fourth consecutive quarter of growth, mainland China −20%**.
- **2026Q1** — **Returns to profit: EPS NT$1.31**; operating margin **8.0%**, gross margin **61.1%**; revenue decline narrows from **−20.7% (March) to −4.2% (June)** as the smaller store base annualises.

Gourmet Master's accounts show a profitable core business that was being drained by one geography — and the cost of stopping it.

- **A restructuring charge that defined the year.** **2025Q3 produced a loss of NT$1.09bn (EPS −NT$6.06)** from **over NT$1bn of one-time impairment** on closing roughly **180 China stores and two central kitchens**. That single quarter turned FY2025 negative: **EPS −NT$2.47**, against **NT$3.28 in FY2024**.
- **The underlying business is not the problem.** **Gross margin is ~61%** — normal and healthy for a bakery-cafe operation — and **operating margin recovered to 8.0% in 2026Q1**, with **2025Q3's −6.1% operating margin** being the restructuring quarter. The company earned **NT$1.31 per share in 2026Q1**.
- **A conservative balance sheet.** **NT$17.4bn of assets** against **NT$10.4bn of equity** and a **40.2% debt ratio**, with **NT$2.5bn of cash** and **positive operating cash flow (NT$0.48bn in the quarter)**. The restructuring was affordable; it did not threaten solvency.
- **The dividend has been suspended.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year) ran **NT$6.0 (2017) → 5.0 → 3.0 (2019) → 4.0 → 5.0 (2021) → 2.5 (2022) → 3.5 (2023) → 3.0 (2024)** — and then stopped. For a consumer company that had paid consistently, this is the clearest signal of how serious the reset was.
- **Priced at book.** **NT$61.90 against a P/B of 1.08×**, with a **return on equity of −3.9%** (still reflecting the loss year). The reported **price/earnings ratio of 0.00 is meaningless against a loss** and has been removed from this page.

The financing reality: **a financially sound company that took a large, deliberate write-off to stop a four-year bleed** — with the balance sheet intact and the recovery, so far, one quarter old.

**Stance: a genuinely strong brand whose Taiwanese and American businesses work, finally cutting a Chinese operation that lost money for four straight years — priced at book value, paying nothing, with a repair that is early but visible.**

The bull case:

1. **Two of three markets are healthy.** In local currency, the **United States grew at double digits** and **Taiwan posted a fourth consecutive quarter of growth**. The 85°C format and brand are not broken; one geography was.
2. **The restructuring is decisive rather than gradual.** Closing **~180 of ~440 China stores**, two central kitchens, and consolidating distribution from **eight centres to three**, with the impairment taken in one quarter, is a real amputation rather than a hope. Management sees a chance for China to **escape four consecutive years of losses**.
3. **Early evidence of repair, at an undemanding price.** **2026Q1 EPS of NT$1.31**, operating margin back to **8.0%**, revenue decline narrowing from **−20.7% to −4.2%**, with the stock at **1.08× book**.

The counter-arguments:

- **The recovery is one quarter old.** FY2025 was a **loss of NT$2.47 per share** and the **dividend is suspended**. Nothing yet proves the smaller China business is durably profitable.
- **Revenue is still declining.** Fewer stores means less revenue; the group must show that **profitability improves faster than revenue shrinks**.
- **China remains difficult.** The competitive and consumer conditions that caused the losses — aggressive local chains, price competition, weak spending — have not changed. A smaller footprint reduces exposure; it does not create an advantage.
- **No income while waiting.** With the dividend suspended, the entire return depends on earnings recovery.

A **restructuring** thesis: buy a healthy brand at book value on the expectation that removing a loss-maker restores group profitability — with the proof still outstanding.

85°C operates a **bakery-cafe chain**, and its economics are those of high-frequency, low-ticket food retail:

- **The format.** Bright, high-traffic stores selling **affordable coffee alongside a broad bakery counter** — cakes, breads and pastries — designed for **daily repeat visits** rather than occasional destination dining. The signature sea-salt coffee and accessible cake pricing built habitual traffic in Taiwan.
- **Why gross margin is ~61%.** Food and beverage prepared in-house carries **high gross margins on ingredients**; the real costs are **rent, labour and logistics**, which sit below the gross line. This is why the **operating margin is only ~8%** even with a 61% gross margin — the business is a **fixed-cost, footfall-driven** operation, and store-level economics depend almost entirely on **sales per store**.
- **Central kitchens and distribution are the hidden infrastructure.** Fresh bakery products require **central production and frequent distribution**, which means a chain must have **enough store density in each region** to make the kitchen and logistics economic. This is precisely what failed in China: stores spread across Beijing, Shandong, Chengdu and Chongqing could not support **eight distribution centres and two central kitchens** — which is why the restructuring cut both stores **and** infrastructure together.
- **Three geographies, three different businesses.** **Taiwan** is mature, dense and growing again; the **United States** is growing at double digits with less direct competition in the format; **mainland China** faced intense local competition and weak spending, and is now being shrunk to a defensible core.

The levers are **same-store sales, store count by geography, central-kitchen and distribution utilisation, and input costs**. The strength is a **real consumer brand with proven format economics where density exists**; the lesson of the last four years is that **a bakery chain cannot be scaled faster than the logistics network that supplies it can be filled.**

Bakery-cafe retail is a business of **density, habit and logistics**, and the three markets 85°C operates in behave very differently.

- **Taiwan: mature but defensible.** High urban density, an entrenched coffee-drinking habit and a well-developed convenience-store sector (7-ELEVEN and FamilyMart both sell coffee aggressively) make it competitive — but 85°C's brand, bakery breadth and store network give it a durable position, evidenced by **four consecutive quarters of growth**.
- **China: the hardest possible market.** The last decade saw an explosion of domestic coffee and bakery chains competing ferociously on price, backed by capital and expanding at extraordinary speed, while **consumer spending weakened**. A foreign-brand chain with a mid-price positioning found itself squeezed between cheaper local operators and premium international ones. **A 20% revenue decline** in that environment, after **four years of losses**, is the outcome of structure rather than execution alone.
- **The United States: a genuine opportunity.** The Asian-style bakery-cafe format has **far less direct competition**, and 85°C has built a real following. **Double-digit growth** suggests the format travels better to a market where it is differentiated than to one where it is undercut.
- **The structural constraint everywhere.** Fresh bakery requires **central kitchens and daily distribution**, so profitability depends on **regional store density**. Chains that expand geographically faster than they densify end up carrying logistics costs that the store base cannot support — the precise trap that the China restructuring is unwinding.

85°C's position is **strong in Taiwan, promising in the US, and now deliberately smaller in China**. The industry truth is that **food chains export brands more easily than they export unit economics** — and the last four years were the cost of learning it.

**Strengths**
- **A genuine consumer brand** (85°C) with proven format economics and habitual traffic; **~61% gross margin**.
- **Two healthy geographies**: **US growing double digits**, **Taiwan in a fourth consecutive quarter of growth**.
- **Sound balance sheet** (40.2% debt ratio, NT$2.5bn cash, positive operating cash flow) that absorbed a **NT$1bn+ impairment** without distress.

**Weaknesses**
- **FY2025 loss of NT$2.47 per share** and a **suspended dividend**.
- **China lost money for four consecutive years** and still declined 20%.
- **Revenue still falling** as ~180 closed stores annualise; low ~8% operating margin.

**Opportunities**
- **China returning to profit** on a smaller, denser, defensible base after closures.
- **US expansion**, where the format is differentiated and growing at double digits.
- Improved central-kitchen and distribution utilisation (8 centres cut to 3).

**Threats**
- Continued intense competition and weak consumer spending in China.
- Rent, labour and ingredient cost inflation compressing an 8% operating margin.
- Convenience-store and chain coffee competition in Taiwan.

- **The China restructuring may not be enough (the central risk).** Closing **~180 of ~440 stores** reduces losses but does not change the competitive environment that caused them — aggressive local chains, price competition and weak consumer spending persist. If the remaining base still cannot earn, further closures and impairments would follow.
- **The recovery is only one quarter old.** **2026Q1's NT$1.31 per share** is encouraging, but FY2025 was a **loss of NT$2.47** and the **dividend is suspended**. Nothing yet demonstrates durable group profitability.
- **Revenue is shrinking by design.** With fewer stores, revenue continues to fall year-on-year (**−4.2% in June**, improved from −20.7% in March). The company must show that **profit recovers faster than revenue declines** — otherwise it has simply become smaller.
- **Thin operating margins.** At **~8%**, store-level economics leave little room for rent, wage or ingredient inflation, and depend heavily on **sales per store**.
- **No dividend while waiting.** The entire return now depends on earnings recovery, with no income to compensate for the wait.
- **Execution across three very different markets.** Taiwan, the US and China require different formats, supply chains and competitive responses; management attention and capital must be split.

Gourmet Master's outlook is a straightforward test of whether **removing a loss-maker restores the profitability of a fundamentally sound business.** The axes to watch:

- **Does China stop losing money?** The decisive question. Management sees a chance for the Chinese business to **escape four consecutive years of losses** on a smaller base with consolidated kitchens and distribution. Confirmation would transform the group's earnings; failure would mean further closures.
- **US growth.** The clearest positive in the business — **double-digit growth** in a market where the bakery-cafe format is differentiated rather than undercut. Whether this can scale into a genuine third pillar matters more to the long-run story than anything in China.
- **Taiwan's momentum.** A **fourth consecutive quarter of growth** in the home market provides the stable cash base that funded the restructuring; sustaining it is essential.
- **Profit versus shrinking revenue.** Revenue will keep declining as closures annualise. The test is **operating margin (now 8.0%)** rising as the drag is removed — and, eventually, the **resumption of a dividend**.

Bottom line: Gourmet Master owns a **real consumer brand in 85°C**, with a **healthy Taiwanese business, a double-digit-growth US business**, and a **Chinese operation that lost money for four consecutive years and has now been cut by roughly 40%** at a cost of **over NT$1bn in impairment**, an **FY2025 loss of NT$2.47 per share** and a **suspended dividend**. The **2026Q1 return to profit (NT$1.31)** and narrowing revenue decline are early evidence that the amputation is working. Judge it on **China reaching breakeven, US expansion, and operating margin** — a sound brand at book value, in the first quarter of proving that its most expensive mistake is behind it.
